newsitem.title: UK: Britain refuses death certificate for Rudolf Hess.
newsitem.headline: Britain refuses death certificate for Rudolf Hess.

text.p: Britain has cancelled the death certificate it issued when Hitler's former deputy Rudolf Hess died in jail in 1987 and it refused to issue another, the Defence Ministry said on Thursday.
It said the government concluded there was never a legal basis for it to register Hess's death even though he died in Spandau prison in what was then the British sector of Berlin.
Hess, who was the last inmate of Spandau, was arrested after he flew to Scotland in May 1941 in an apparent attempt to negotiate a truce between Britain and Germany.
Rhodri Morgan, an opposition Labour member of Britain's parliament who has taken a close interest in the circumstances of Hess's death, condemned the decision.
"As far as the British government is concerned, Hess is still alive. That is clearly absurd. The British government has got to do something to correct that absurdity," he told Reuters.

Morgan said the refusal to issue a new certificate was likely to reinforce speculation that Hess had not committed suicide as was stated at the time but had been put to death by Britain or her allies.

In a written parliamentary answer to a question from Morgan, Nicholas Soames, a minister at the defence ministry, recalled that in 1995 Hess' son, Wolf Ruediger Hess, applied for an amendment to the register in which his father's death is recorded.
Hess's family challenges the official version that as a frail 93-year-old in August, 1987, he hanged himself in a summer house in the grounds of the prison where he was the only inmate.
The summer house burned down, making it impossible to find the noose Hess was supposed to have used.

Soames said that when Wolf Hess made his application, it was realised that the registration of his father's death was not in accordance with the law, which dealt only with the deaths of British servicemen, their families and associated civilians.
"Since Rudolf Hess belonged to none of the categories specified in the legislation, the question of a new entry, in any form, does not arise," he said.

But Morgan described the decision as "British bureaucracy at its worst". "Any belief that this lays the case to rest is just a complete nonsense," he said, adding Britain had a moral obligation to clear the matter up even if it had no legal one.

He said there was reason to believe that in 1987, Russia, which had for years insisted Hess must be kept in Spandau, was about to relent and agree he should be allowed to spend the remainder of his days in freedom.
This may have alarmed some in British ruling circles who had feared Hess would then be free to reveal the reason he flew to Scotland in 1941.
"It is not possible at this stage to say definitely that Hess committed suicide," Morgan said.

A defence ministry spokeswoman, asked who was responsible for registering Hess's death if it was not a matter for Britain, replied: "That is one of the things we are trying to establish at the moment."
